options.B: S$900 per policy year
options.C: No limit; the whole component is MediSave-payable
options.D: S$300 per policy year

explanation: The AWL by Age Next Birthday is S$300 (up to 40), S$600 (41 to 70), and S$900 (71 and above). An insured aged 55 falls in the 41 to 70 band, so the AWL is S$600 per policy year, with any excess paid in cash.

stem: For an inpatient hospital stay, the MediSave daily withdrawal limit for ward and treatment charges is set at which amounts?

options.A: Up to S$550 per day for the first two days, then S$400 per day thereafter
options.B: Up to S$800 per day for every day of the stay
options.C: Up to S$300 per day for every day of the stay
options.D: Up to S$400 per day for the first two days, then S$550 per day thereafter

explanation: The MediSave inpatient daily limit is up to S$550 per day for the first two days and S$400 per day thereafter. Day surgery has a separate limit of up to S$300 per day.

stem: CareShield Life offers means-tested premium subsidies of up to what percentage of base premiums for lower- to middle-income households?

options.A: Up to 10% of base premiums
options.B: Up to 30% of base premiums
options.C: Up to 75% of base premiums
options.D: Up to 50% of base premiums

explanation: CareShield Life provides means-tested premium subsidies of up to 30% of base premiums. This contrasts with the MediShield Life income-based subsidy of up to 50% of premiums.

stem: For CareShield Life, how long must a member pay premiums, and how long do they remain insured?

options.A: Premiums for life, and insured for life
options.B: Premiums until age 67 or for 10 years, whichever is shorter, and insured until age 67
options.C: Premiums until age 67 or for 10 years, whichever is longer, but insured for life
options.D: Premiums for exactly 5 years, and insured for 60 months only

explanation: CareShield Life members pay premiums until the year they reach age 67 or for 10 years, whichever is longer, but remain insured for life.

stem: Which of these premiums are FULLY payable by MediSave without a withdrawal limit?

options.A: ElderShield/CareShield Life Supplements and IP riders
options.B: Integrated Shield Plan private components and IP riders
options.C: MediShield Life and ElderShield/CareShield Life premiums
options.D: IP riders only

explanation: MediShield Life and ElderShield/CareShield Life premiums are fully payable by MediSave. Integrated Shield Plans and ElderShield/CareShield Life Supplements are subject to withdrawal limits, and IP riders are cash-only.

stem: The Majulah Package targets Young Seniors born in which years?

options.A: Born 1960 to 1973
options.B: Born on or before 1949
options.C: Born 1950 to 1959
options.D: Born 1974 to 1985

explanation: The Majulah Package (introduced 2023) targets Young Seniors born 1960 to 1973, extended to all Singapore Citizens born in 1973 or earlier, and includes Earn and Save, Retirement Savings and MediSave Bonus components.

stem: A Singapore Citizen aged 62 is admitted to a Class B2 ward for 10 days. Daily ward and treatment charges are S$1,000 per day (S$10,000 total), with no surgery. Using Appendix 9B figures (Normal Ward limit S$800/day, deductible S$2,000, co-insurance 10%/5%/3%), how much does MediShield Life pay?
explanation: Claimable is capped at S$800 x 10 = S$8,000 (lower than the S$10,000 actual). Less the S$2,000 deductible leaves S$6,000. Co-insurance: the first S$5,000 band less deductible is S$3,000 at 10% = S$300; the remaining S$3,000 (from S$5,000 to S$8,000) at 5% = S$150; total S$450. Payout = S$8,000 - S$2,000 - S$450 = S$5,550.

stem: A Singapore Citizen aged 60 stays in a Class A ward (pro-ration factor 35%). Normal-ward charges are S$1,500 per day for 10 days (S$15,000 actual), no surgery. Using Appendix 9B figures (S$800/day limit, deductible S$2,000, co-insurance tiers 10%/5%/3%), what is the MediShield Life payout?
explanation: Pro-rate first: 35% of S$15,000 = S$5,250, which is below the ward limit of S$800 x 10 = S$8,000, so claimable is S$5,250. Less the S$2,000 deductible leaves S$3,250. Co-insurance on the amount above the deductible: S$3,000 sits in the first S$5,000 band at 10% = S$300, and the remaining S$250 (from S$5,000 to S$5,250) at 5% = S$12.50, total S$312.50. Payout = S$5,250 - S$2,000 - S$312.50 = S$2,937.50.

stem: A patient's MediShield Life claimable amount (after any pro-ration, before deductible) totals S$12,000 for the policy year. The deductible is S$2,000 (Class B2, age below 80). Applying the co-insurance tiers of 10%/5%/3%, what is the total co-insurance the patient bears?
explanation: Co-insurance is applied to the claimable amount above the deductible, split by band. First S$5,000 band less deductible S$2,000 = S$3,000 at 10% = S$300; next S$5,000 (S$5,000 to S$10,000) at 5% = S$250; above S$10,000 is S$12,000 - S$10,000 = S$2,000 at 3% = S$60. Total co-insurance = S$300 + S$250 + S$60 = S$610.

stem: A CareShield Life policyholder is assessed as severely disabled and receives the base payout of S$600 per month. Ignoring any annual increase, how much does she receive over 8 months of continuous severe disability?
explanation: CareShield Life pays at least S$600 per month for as long as severe disability persists. Over 8 months: S$600 x 8 = S$4,800.

stem: A member is hospitalised for 5 days. The ward and treatment charges portion of his bill is S$3,000. Applying only the MediSave inpatient daily limits (S$550 per day for the first two days, S$400 per day thereafter), what is the maximum he may withdraw from MediSave for these daily charges?
explanation: First two days at S$550 = S$1,100; remaining three days at S$400 = S$1,200; total limit = S$2,300. This is below the S$3,000 charges, so the withdrawal is capped at S$2,300 and the balance is paid by cash or other means.

stem: A patient with an Integrated Shield Plan rider requiring a minimum 5% co-payment (co-payment cap S$3,000 per policy year) receives panel, pre-authorised treatment costing S$40,000. What is the patient's co-payment?
explanation: The minimum 5% co-payment on S$40,000 is S$2,000, which is below the S$3,000 cap. So the patient pays S$2,000. The cap only bites once 5% of the bill exceeds S$3,000 (that is, bills above S$60,000).

stem: The additional private insurance component of an IP premium is S$1,000 for an insured aged 55 (Age Next Birthday). Given the AWL of S$600 for the 41 to 70 age band, how much of this component is payable by MediSave and how much in cash?

options.A: S$400 by MediSave and S$600 in cash
options.B: S$300 by MediSave and S$700 in cash
options.C: S$600 by MediSave and S$400 in cash
options.D: S$1,000 fully by MediSave and S$0 in cash

explanation: For an insured aged 55, the AWL is S$600. MediSave pays up to the AWL of S$600, and the excess of S$1,000 - S$600 = S$400 must be paid in cash.

stem: A claimant under ElderShield400 receives the full monthly benefit for the entire maximum payout period. What is the total maximum amount payable under ElderShield400?
explanation: ElderShield400 pays S$400 per month for up to 72 months. Maximum total = S$400 x 72 = S$28,800. (ElderShield300 pays S$300 x 60 = S$18,000.)

stem: Which of the following is a standard section of a Health Insurance policy contract?

options.A: Actuarial Valuation Report
options.B: Shareholders' Dividend Schedule
options.C: Investment Performance Statement
options.D: Insuring Clause and Definitions

explanation: The standard sections include the Policy Schedule, Insuring Clause and Definitions, General Conditions, Benefit Provisions, Exclusions, Claim Conditions and Endorsements. The section order may vary by insurer.

stem: Under the definitions in a typical Health Insurance policy, an insured child is defined as being below what age, with an extension for full-time students?

options.A: Below 16 years, extended to 21 if in full-time education
options.B: Below 18 years, extended to 21 if in full-time education
options.C: Below 21 years, extended to 25 if in full-time recognised higher education
options.D: Below 25 years, with no extension for students

explanation: An insured child is defined as below 21 years old, or up to 25 if in full-time recognised higher education.

stem: Which of the following would NOT be considered medically necessary treatment?

options.A: A routine health screening ordered for preventive purposes
options.B: Diagnosis of an illness using generally accepted medical practices
options.C: Direct treatment of a diagnosed illness that is cost-effective
options.D: Care consistent with current professional standards for a disability

explanation: Medically necessary treatment excludes care for prevention, health screening or promoting good health. A doctor prescribing something does not by itself make it medically necessary.

stem: The definition of a pre-existing condition includes an objective element. What is it?

options.A: What a reasonable and sensible person would have done to get medical advice or treatment
options.B: Whether treatment cost more than the policy deductible
options.C: Whether the condition was listed by MOH as serious
options.D: Whether the insurer's doctor personally examined the insured

explanation: The test is not only what the insured actually knew but also what a reasonable and sensible person would have done to seek medical advice or treatment before the policy issue or reinstatement date.

stem: In Disability Income Insurance, the waiting period, during which benefits are not payable, is measured from what point and is also known by which name?

options.A: From the first ADL failure; also called the incontestability period
options.B: From the onset of disability; also called the elimination or probationary period
options.C: From the date of claim; also called the free-look period
options.D: From policy issue; also called the deferred period

explanation: In Disability Income Insurance the waiting period runs from the onset of disability and is called the elimination or probationary period. In Medical Expense Insurance it runs from policy issue (illness only); in Long-Term Care it runs from the first ADL failure (deferred period).

stem: The general free-look period for a Health Insurance policy allows the owner to review and return it for a refund up to how many days from receipt, and within how many days is the document deemed received?

options.A: Up to 30 days from receipt; deemed received within 7 days of despatch
options.B: Up to 14 days from receipt; deemed received within 7 days of despatch
options.C: Up to 60 days from receipt; deemed received within 14 days of despatch
options.D: Up to 14 days from receipt; deemed received within 14 days of despatch

explanation: The general free-look period is up to 14 days from receipt, with the policy deemed received within 7 days of despatch. This differs from ElderShield and CareShield Life, which have a 60-day free-look period.

stem: For emergency overseas treatment that is covered, how much will the insurer pay?

options.A: The full actual overseas expenses regardless of local cost
options.B: Always the Singapore-equivalent cost even if actual cost is lower
options.C: A fixed daily allowance unrelated to the actual expenses
options.D: The lower of the actual overseas expenses or the Singapore-equivalent reasonable expenses

explanation: Both emergency and planned overseas treatment (where covered) pay the lower of the actual overseas cost or the reasonable expenses that would have been paid for equivalent treatment in a Singapore hospital.

stem: Under a Guaranteed Renewable basis, what is the ONLY reason the insurer may cancel the policy?

options.A: The insured changing to a more hazardous occupation
options.B: The insurer deciding to exit the market
options.C: Deterioration in the insured's health
options.D: Non-payment of premium

explanation: On a Guaranteed Renewable basis the insurer gives up the right to cancel or refuse renewal, and non-payment of premium is the only reason for cancellation. Premiums may still be increased, but only on a class basis.

stem: The general grace period to pay a renewal premium for most Health Insurance policies is how long?

options.A: 14 days
options.B: 30 days
options.C: 75 days
options.D: 60 days

explanation: The general grace period is 30 days for most policies, with coverage remaining in force during it. This contrasts with ElderShield's 75-day grace period.

stem: Under a Change of Occupation provision in a Disability Income policy, what happens if the insured moves to a MORE hazardous occupation?

options.A: The insurer may reduce the maximum benefit amount
options.B: The policy is automatically cancelled
options.C: The insurer must reduce the premium
options.D: The insurer must increase the benefit amount

explanation: Moving to a more hazardous occupation lets the insurer reduce the maximum benefit amount. Moving to a less hazardous occupation instead reduces the premium.

stem: The Co-ordination of Benefits (Over-insurance or Contribution) provision applies in which circumstance?

options.A: Only for death benefit claims
options.B: Only when the insured has no other insurance at all
options.C: Even if the insurer was not notified of the insured's other coverage
options.D: Only if the insured disclosed all other coverage at application

explanation: Co-ordination of Benefits prevents profiting from a claim and applies whether or not the insurer was notified of other coverage. The insurer may even demand return of benefits already paid if it later learns of other sources.

stem: Under the Last Payer Status provision in MediShield Life and Private IPs, what must the insured do before claiming?

options.A: First exhaust their entire MediSave balance
options.B: First apply to MediFund for assistance
options.C: First pay the full bill in cash and seek reimbursement later
options.D: First claim from other medical insurance or employee benefits

explanation: Last Payer Status means MediShield Life or a Private IP pays last. The insured must first claim from other medical insurance or employee benefits before claiming under MediShield Life or a Private IP.

stem: Under the Nomination of Beneficiaries framework, a Section 132 nomination (Trust/Irrevocable) has what effect on the policyowner?

options.A: The policyowner retains ownership and can change nominees freely
options.B: The policyowner loses all ownership rights and needs all nominees' consent to revoke
options.C: The policyowner may revoke only with the insurer's consent
options.D: The policyowner keeps ownership but cannot borrow against the policy

explanation: A Section 132 Trust/Irrevocable nomination means the policyowner loses all ownership rights and needs the written consent of all nominees to revoke. A Section 133 Revocable nomination lets the owner retain ownership and change nominees freely.

stem: The Policy Owners' Protection (PPF) Scheme is administered by which body, and how is coverage obtained?

options.A: The CPF Board, with automatic coverage
options.B: The Agency for Integrated Care (AIC), by application
options.C: The Singapore Deposit Insurance Corporation (SDIC), with automatic coverage
options.D: The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), by application

explanation: The PPF Scheme is administered by the SDIC and coverage is automatic with no action needed by policy owners. MAS supervises insurers but does not guarantee individual institutions.

stem: Under the Claim Conditions of a policy, who bears the expense of submitting the required claim certificates, forms, bills and receipts?

options.A: The government, through MediFund
options.B: The hospital, which absorbs all costs
options.C: The policy owner, at his own expense
options.D: The insurer, in every case

explanation: The policy owner must, at his own expense, submit the certificates, forms, original bills, receipts and evidence required. Submission may be made electronically by a hospital or clinic via the MediClaim system.

stem: In the dispute resolution process for a Health Insurance claim, which body should a dispute be referred to FIRST, and within what time?

options.A: The High Court, within one year
options.B: The Singapore International Arbitration Centre, within 30 days
options.C: MAS, within 60 days
options.D: FIDReC, within six months of the failure to reach agreement with the insurer

explanation: A dispute should first go to the Financial Industry Disputes Resolution Centre (FIDReC), referred within six months of the failure to reach agreement. If it cannot be dealt with there it goes to arbitration under the SIAC, and only then to legal action.

stem: An endorsement on a Health Insurance policy can serve which of the following functions?

options.A: Either add optional benefits for an extra premium, or restrict coverage by excluding a condition
options.B: Only cancel the entire policy
options.C: Only change the identity of the insured
options.D: Only add benefits, never restrict coverage

explanation: An endorsement can add optional benefits (requiring an additional premium) or restrict coverage by excluding a specific pre-existing condition or activity. An exclusion endorsement can be a counter-offer that becomes binding once the insured signs and accepts.

stem: How does a Per Policy Year Limit differ from a Lifetime Limit in a Medical Expense Insurance policy?

options.A: The Per Policy Year Limit resets each year, while the Lifetime Limit is cumulative over the whole policy
options.B: Both reset each year
options.C: The Per Policy Year Limit is cumulative, while the Lifetime Limit resets each year
options.D: Both are cumulative over the whole policy

explanation: The Per Policy Year Limit is the maximum paid for eligible expenses in each policy year and resets annually. The Lifetime Limit is the maximum paid over the entire life of the policy and is cumulative.

stem: A Medical Expense Insurance plan entitles the insured to a standard B1 ward but he is admitted to a private hospital (pro-ration factor 35%). His total bill is S$24,000. The plan has an annual deductible of S$3,500 and 10% co-insurance. How much does the insurer pay?
explanation: Pro-rate first: 35% of S$24,000 = S$8,400. Less the S$3,500 deductible leaves S$4,900. Co-insurance is 10% x (S$8,400 - S$3,500) = S$490. Insurer pays S$8,400 - S$3,500 - S$490 = S$4,410. The insured bears the balance out of pocket.

stem: Which measure is the PRIMARY consideration when pricing a Health Insurance policy?

options.A: Morbidity, the rate at which illness occurs within a group over time
options.B: Mortality, the incidence of death within a group
options.C: The insurer's target profit margin
options.D: The persistency rate of the portfolio

explanation: Health Insurance is priced on morbidity, the incidence of illness within a group over a period. Mortality is the measure used for Life Insurance.

stem: For most Health Insurance policies, why do women generally pay higher premium rates than men of the same age?

options.A: Women have a higher mortality rate than men
options.B: Women, on average, have a higher morbidity rate and make more medical claims
options.C: Regulations require insurers to cross-subsidise male policyholders
options.D: Women tend to have poorer persistency than men

explanation: On average the morbidity rate of women is higher and they make more medical claims, so they pay higher premiums for most Health Insurance products.

stem: What effect does investment income earned on premiums have on the price an insurer charges?

options.A: It increases premiums because the insurer must share returns
options.B: It has no effect on premiums, only on shareholder profit
options.C: It reduces the premiums the insurer needs to charge
options.D: It only affects group plans, not individual plans

explanation: Surplus premiums not needed for that year's claims are invested to earn more; this investment income is an additional source of funds that helps reduce premiums.

stem: A Health & Surgical plan is redesigned with a SMALLER deductible and SMALLER co-insurance. What is the effect on the premium?

options.A: The premium falls because the insured bears less
options.B: The premium falls only for public hospital coverage
options.C: The premium is unchanged since deductibles do not affect pricing
options.D: The premium rises because the insurer bears more of each claim

explanation: A smaller deductible and smaller co-insurance shift more of the claim cost to the insurer, so the premium rises. Larger deductibles and co-insurance lower the premium.

stem: An insurer chooses to reduce the number of health declarations on its proposal form to speed up sales. How does this affect the premium?

options.A: The premium is higher because the insurer takes on more unknown risk
options.B: The premium is lower because underwriting costs fall
options.C: The premium is unaffected because underwriting does not influence price
options.D: The premium is lower only for younger applicants

explanation: Doing minimal risk assessment means the insurer accepts more unknown risk, so it charges a higher premium to compensate.

stem: How does a more frequent premium payment mode (e.g. monthly versus annually) affect the total premium paid over a year?

options.A: It slightly lowers the total premium as a loyalty discount
options.B: It slightly raises the total premium to recover billing costs and lost investment income
options.C: It has no effect on the total premium
options.D: It halves the total premium under a semi-annual mode

explanation: More frequent payment slightly raises the total premium because the insurer must recover extra handling costs and the investment income lost from not receiving the full annual premium upfront.

stem: Which of the following Health Insurance premiums are based on AGE only and are NOT differentiated by gender?

options.A: Long-Term Care and Critical Illness premiums
options.B: Disability Income Insurance premiums
options.C: MediShield Life and Integrated Shield Plan premiums
options.D: All Health Insurance premiums are gender-differentiated

explanation: For simplicity, MediShield Life and Integrated Shield Plan premiums depend on age but not gender, unlike most other Health Insurance products.

stem: According to the pricing chapter, which single LIFESTYLE factor is the most important in determining a Health Insurance premium rate?

options.A: Participation in mountaineering
options.B: Alcohol consumption
options.C: Recreational scuba-diving
options.D: Smoking

explanation: Smoking is the most important lifestyle factor for pricing; a non-smoker pays a lower premium than a smoker.

stem: If an insurer expects the persistency of a block of Health Insurance business to be HIGH, what will it do to the premium?

options.A: Reduce the premium charged
options.B: Increase the premium to reflect longer exposure
options.C: Leave the premium unchanged
options.D: Apply a persistency loading

explanation: High expected persistency lets the insurer spread costs over more renewal years, so it reduces the premium charged.

stem: Which statement about persistency across age groups is correct?

options.A: Older insureds always lapse first because premiums are higher
options.B: Younger insureds (ages 20-29) tend to have poorer persistency than older insureds (ages 50-59)
options.C: Persistency is identical across all age groups
options.D: Persistency worsens as a policy ages

explanation: Younger insureds tend to have poorer persistency; older insureds value the cover more since they may struggle to satisfy underwriting for a new policy. Persistency usually improves as a policy ages.

stem: The total claims of a portfolio comprise paid claims, pending claims and one further component. What does IBNR stand for?

options.A: Insured But Not Refunded
options.B: Investigated But Not Resolved
options.C: Incurred But Not Reported
options.D: Indemnified But Not Recorded

explanation: IBNR means Incurred But Not Reported: the loss has already occurred but has not yet been reported to the insurer, so a reserve must be estimated for it.

stem: In a voluntary group plan, why does LOW employee participation increase pricing risk?

options.A: It dilutes healthy lives with too many claims-free members
options.B: It guarantees a good mix of healthy lives
options.C: It reduces administration costs so premiums must rise
options.D: It raises anti-selection risk as unhealthy individuals self-select into cover

explanation: Low participation raises anti-selection: a higher-than-normal proportion of individuals with health issues seek the cover. High participation dilutes this with healthy lives.

stem: Which of the following best describes the driver behind medical inflation that insurers must factor into pricing?

options.A: A consistent upward trend from rising medical charges, medical advancement and higher utilisation, especially with an ageing population
options.B: A one-off spike caused solely by a single pandemic
options.C: A fall in claim costs as technology improves efficiency
options.D: A regulated annual cap set by MAS

explanation: Medical inflation is the consistent upward trend in claim costs driven by rising charges, medical advancement and higher utilisation amid an ageing population.

stem: A group Health Insurance portfolio has earned premiums of S$1,200,000 for the year. Paid claims are S$700,000, pending claims are S$90,000 and estimated IBNR is S$50,000. What is the incurred claims ratio (loss ratio)?
explanation: Total incurred claims = paid + pending + IBNR = 700,000 + 90,000 + 50,000 = S$840,000. Loss ratio = 840,000 / 1,200,000 = 70.0%. Omitting IBNR would wrongly give about 65.8%.

stem: An insurer targets a claims (loss) ratio of no more than 75%. For a block with earned premium of S$1,000,000, total incurred claims are: paid S$600,000, pending S$90,000 and IBNR S$60,000. Does the block meet the target, and what is the ratio?

options.A: Yes; the ratio is 69.0% once IBNR is excluded
options.B: No; the ratio is 82.5%
options.C: Yes; the ratio is exactly 75.0%
options.D: No; the ratio is 90.0%

explanation: Incurred claims = 600,000 + 90,000 + 60,000 = S$750,000. Ratio = 750,000 / 1,000,000 = 75.0%, exactly meeting the target. IBNR must be included in incurred claims.

stem: Health Insurance underwriting is concerned primarily with which measure of risk?

options.A: Mortality
options.B: Investment yield
options.C: Lapse rate
options.D: Morbidity

explanation: Health Insurance underwriting assesses morbidity, the rate of disease or illness in a group over time, whereas Life Insurance underwriting is concerned with mortality.

stem: For Disability Income Insurance, the benefit amount applied for must not exceed what proportion of the life insured's current income?
explanation: The DII benefit ceiling is 75% of current income, to preserve the insured's incentive to return to work and avoid over-insurance.

stem: Which is the correct default position on which underwriting approach an adviser should start with?

options.A: Moratorium underwriting, for the client's convenience
options.B: Full Medical Underwriting should always be the starting point
options.C: Guaranteed Issuance Offer, to avoid declines
options.D: Simplified Issuance Offer, to speed up issuance

explanation: Full Medical Underwriting should always be the starting point; it gives the insured certainty about what is covered at the outset. Advisers must not default to moratorium merely for convenience.

stem: Under Moratorium (Point-of-Claim) Underwriting, when will a pre-existing condition present at the commencement date become covered?

options.A: Immediately, since no health declaration was taken
options.B: Never, because moratorium excludes all conditions permanently
options.C: Only if the insured has no symptom, treatment, medication or advice for it during the waiting period
options.D: After a fixed 12-month period regardless of symptoms

explanation: The pre-existing condition is excluded at the outset and only becomes covered once the waiting period (usually two to five years) is satisfied symptom, treatment and advice free.

stem: Under Moratorium Underwriting, how are long-term conditions such as stroke, kidney failure or dementia that need continuous treatment handled?

options.A: They are covered as soon as the moratorium period ends
options.B: They are covered after a doubled waiting period
options.C: They are covered from day one
options.D: They will never be covered, as they cannot meet the symptom-free condition

explanation: Long-term conditions needing continuous treatment can never satisfy the symptom, treatment and advice free requirement, so they are never covered under a moratorium.

stem: What distinguishes a Guaranteed Issuance Offer (GIO) from a Simplified Issuance Offer (SIO)?

options.A: GIO asks no medical questions at all, whereas SIO asks a few questions
options.B: SIO asks no medical questions, whereas GIO asks a few
options.C: Both require a full medical examination
options.D: GIO offers larger cover with no exclusions

explanation: GIO requires no medical questions and guarantees issue subject to eligibility (usually an age limit), while SIO asks a few questions whose answers determine approval.

stem: To minimise anti-selection, GIO policies typically carry which features?

options.A: Large cover with no exclusions
options.B: Smaller coverage with pre-existing conditions permanently excluded
options.C: Full cover after a two-year moratorium
options.D: Cover only for accidental causes

explanation: GIO policies limit anti-selection by offering smaller coverage and permanently excluding pre-existing conditions; premiums are higher for the guaranteed convenience.

stem: For a contributory (voluntary) group plan, what minimum participation of eligible members do insurers typically require to guard against anti-selection?
explanation: Insurers normally require a minimum participation of typically 70% to 90% of eligible members on contributory group plans to reduce anti-selection and administration costs.

stem: What is the free cover limit in group underwriting?

options.A: The maximum cover the insurer will offer any group in total
options.B: The premium refunded when a member leaves
options.C: The waiting period before a member's cover starts
options.D: The maximum coverage granted to each member without a health declaration

explanation: The free cover limit is the maximum coverage granted to each member without requiring a health declaration; any excess above it must be individually underwritten.

stem: Which is the PRIMARY source of underwriting information?

options.A: The Proposal Form
options.B: The Agent's Statement
options.C: The Attending Physician's Statement
options.D: A supplementary lifestyle questionnaire

explanation: The proposal form is the primary source of underwriting information; the APS, agent's statement, exams and questionnaires supplement it when deeper insight is needed.

stem: Who bears the cost of a medical examination required at application?

options.A: Always the applicant
options.B: The insurer, unless the policy is subsequently not taken up
options.C: The attending physician
options.D: Split equally between insurer and applicant

explanation: The insurer bears the exam cost, unless the policy is subsequently not taken up, in which case the applicant bears it.

stem: Because the representative has personal contact with the client, what role is he considered to perform in the underwriting process?

options.A: The chief underwriter
options.B: The claims assessor
options.C: The field underwriter
options.D: The attending physician

explanation: The representative is the field underwriter: best placed to select the client, ensure truthful disclosure and extract full details for any 'Yes' answers on the proposal form.

stem: What proportion of proposals are typically accepted at STANDARD rates?

options.A: About 40% to 50%
options.B: About 60% to 70%
options.C: Effectively 100%
options.D: About 80% to 90%

explanation: Usually 80% to 90% of proposals are accepted at standard rates, and the declination rate is typically below 10%.

stem: Which modification of cover is COMMON in Medical Expense Insurance but rarely used there, being more typical of DII and Critical Illness?

options.A: Specific exclusions are common in Medical Expense; extra premiums are rare there
options.B: Extra premiums are common in Medical Expense; exclusions are rare there
options.C: Both exclusions and extra premiums are equally common in Medical Expense
options.D: Neither is ever used in Medical Expense Insurance

explanation: Specific exclusions (endorsements naming an excluded risk) are common in Medical Expense Insurance, whereas extra premiums are common in DII and Critical Illness but rarely used in Medical Expense.

stem: Which two factors are described as the KEY considerations when underwriting Long-Term Care Insurance?

options.A: Family history and smoking habit
options.B: Detecting early cognitive impairment and assessing morbidity risk (ability to perform ADLs)
options.C: Occupational class and residency
options.D: Income stability and net worth

explanation: The two key LTC underwriting factors are detecting early cognitive impairment and assessing morbidity risk, that is the ability to perform Activities of Daily Living. Family history and smoking are highlighted for Critical Illness.

stem: In group underwriting, why must a group have been formed for a purpose other than only buying insurance?

options.A: To qualify for tax relief
options.B: To satisfy the free cover limit
options.C: To reduce anti-selection
options.D: To guarantee a minimum group size

explanation: The 'reason for existence' requirement reduces anti-selection: members must have joined for a genuine purpose such as running a business, and be actively at work with predictable incomes.

stem: For a SUB-STANDARD risk, when is cover effected and the policy issued?

options.A: Automatically once the proposal form is submitted
options.B: Only after a mandatory 30-day cooling period
options.C: Immediately upon the medical examination
options.D: After the proposer agrees to the terms in the letter of acceptance and pays the premium

explanation: For a sub-standard risk the insurer communicates the terms first; cover is effected and the policy issued once the proposer agrees to those terms and pays the premium.

stem: A self-employed graphic designer earns S$8,000 a month and applies for Disability Income Insurance. Applying the standard income-replacement ceiling, what is the maximum monthly benefit an insurer will allow?
explanation: The DII benefit is capped at 75% of current income: 0.75 x S$8,000 = S$6,000 per month. Insuring the full income would remove the incentive to return to work.

stem: Under which statute is Notice No: MAS 120 issued?

options.A: The Financial Advisers Act 2001
options.B: Sections 67, 72 and 154(4) of the Insurance Act 1966
options.C: The Personal Data Protection Act 2012
options.D: The Securities and Futures Act 2001

explanation: MAS 120 is issued under Sections 67, 72 and 154(4) of the Insurance Act 1966 and covers disclosure and advisory requirements for Accident and Health products.

stem: Which statement about the structure of Notice No: MAS 120 is correct?

options.A: It contains only mandatory requirements
options.B: It contains only best-practice guidance with no binding rules
options.C: It has Part I mandatory requirements and Part II non-mandatory best-practice standards
options.D: It applies solely to group policies

explanation: MAS 120 comprises Part I mandatory requirements and Part II non-mandatory best-practice standards on disclosure and provision of advice for A&H policies.

stem: A direct insurer may use the word 'Shield' in the name or title of a policy only when the policy is which of the following?

options.A: Any personal accident policy
options.B: Any policy with a free-look period
options.C: Any policy sold through a bank
options.D: A Medisave-approved policy

explanation: The word 'Shield' may only be used for a Medisave-approved policy, that is an integrated shield plan, non-integrated shield plan or supplementary disability insurance policy.

stem: In MAS 120 terms, what is the difference between 'switching' and 'upgrading'?

options.A: Switching means replacing a policy with another; upgrading means better benefits with the SAME insurer
options.B: Switching means better benefits with the same insurer; upgrading means replacing with another insurer
options.C: Both mean the same thing
options.D: Switching applies only to group plans; upgrading only to individual plans

explanation: Switching includes terminating a policy and replacing it with another (possibly a different insurer's). Upgrading means varying terms or terminating an existing policy to buy a new one with the same insurer for better benefits.

stem: A 'selected client' under MAS 120 must meet any TWO of three criteria. Which set correctly lists them?

options.A: 65 years or older; unemployed; below diploma level
options.B: 62 years or older; not proficient in spoken or written English; below GCE 'O'/'N' level or equivalent
options.C: 55 years or older; not a Singapore Citizen; below GCE 'A' level
options.D: 62 years or older; low net worth; no existing insurance

explanation: A selected client meets any two of: 62 years or older; not proficient in spoken or written English; below GCE 'O'/'N' level or equivalent education.

stem: Product summaries, conditional offer letters and termination letters for individual medical expense policies must use which minimum font specification?

options.A: Arial 12-point or larger
options.B: Calibri 11-point or larger
options.C: Times New Roman 10-point or larger
options.D: Any legible font of at least 8-point

explanation: MAS 120 requires these documents to use font size Times New Roman 10-point or larger, with standardised disclosure statements.

stem: Where an insurer may vary, amend or add to the terms of an A&H policy, how far in advance must it furnish the policy owner with the change in writing?

options.A: At least 14 days before the change takes effect
options.B: At least 21 days before the change takes effect
options.C: At least 60 days before the change takes effect
options.D: At least 30 days before the change takes effect

explanation: The insurer must disclose the existing and new terms in writing to the policy owner at least 30 days before the change takes effect.

stem: A representative fails to comply with a mandatory requirement in Part I of MAS 120. Under which provision is this an offence?

options.A: Section 142(3) of the Insurance Act 1966
options.B: Section 23(5) of the Insurance Act 1966
options.C: Section 67 of the Insurance Act 1966
options.D: It is not an offence, only a best-practice breach

explanation: Failure to comply with any Part I requirement of MAS 120 is an offence punishable under Section 142(3) of the Insurance Act 1966. Part II is non-mandatory and carries no offence.

stem: When must the intermediary furnish the policy owner with the document summarising the information gathered and the advice provided?

options.A: Within 30 days after the policy is issued
options.B: Before the owner signs the application form
options.C: At the free-look expiry
options.D: Only if the owner requests it

explanation: The documentation of the KYC summary and the advice and its basis must be given to the owner before he signs the application form, not afterwards.

stem: Division 4's reasonable-basis-for-advice requirement does NOT apply in which situation?

options.A: When recommending an Integrated Shield Plan
options.B: When advising a selected client
options.C: When only factual information is provided or advice concerns an ElderShield policy
options.D: When advising on a group medical plan

explanation: Division 4 does not apply where no recommendation is made or only factual information is provided, nor to advice on any ElderShield policy.

stem: Under Division 4's Know-Your-Client requirement for an individual, the information collected must be:

options.A: Collected only, with documentation optional
options.B: Kept verbally by the representative
options.C: Documented only after the sale closes
options.D: Both collected AND documented

explanation: KYC information about objectives, financial situation and needs must be both collected and documented, and items (a)-(e) also apply to any dependants to be insured.

stem: When assessing whether a switch of A&H policy is detrimental to the insured, which of the following is one of the factors MAS has regard to?

options.A: Whether the replacement gives a lower benefit at higher or same cost, or the same benefit at higher cost
options.B: Whether the new insurer has a larger market share
options.C: Whether the representative earns more commission
options.D: Whether the owner prefers the new insurer's brand

explanation: One detriment factor is whether the replacement provides a lower benefit at higher or same cost, or the same benefit at higher cost. Others include penalties, transaction cost without real benefit, and lower suitability.

stem: MAS 120 does NOT apply to A&H policies in which of the following cases?

options.A: Policies sold through a bank branch
options.B: Policies in respect of reinsurance of liabilities, and policies paying A&H benefits only on total and permanent disability
options.C: Policies with a free-look period
options.D: Policies issued to selected clients

explanation: The Notice does not apply where policies are in respect of reinsurance of insurance liabilities, or where A&H benefits are paid only if the insured becomes totally and permanently disabled as defined.

stem: Under the Part II best-practice standard for monitoring switching, who reviews each switching recommendation and indicates in writing whether he agrees, using the same detriment factors?

options.A: The policy owner
options.B: The insurer's chief underwriter
options.C: The representative's supervisor
options.D: An independent MAS officer

explanation: The representative's supervisor should review each switching recommendation and indicate in writing whether he agrees, applying the same para-44 detriment factors used in the mandatory assessment.

stem: For telephone marketing of a NON-Medisave-approved A&H policy where no advice is given and the aim is to close the sale, what must the intermediary do?

options.A: Nothing extra, since no advice is provided
options.B: Refer the recipient to MAS before any sale
options.C: Obtain written consent before dialling
options.D: Warn the recipient he may wish to seek advice first, and keep a record of all calls for audit

explanation: The intermediary must warn the recipient he may wish to seek advice first, that if he does not he should consider suitability himself, and must keep a record of all calls for audit.

stem: Under Division 1A, what must an A&H insurance REPRESENTATIVE disclose in writing to the policy owner?

options.A: His name and the intermediary or intermediaries for which he acts
options.B: His personal home address and salary
options.C: The insurer's reinsurance arrangements
options.D: His past sales performance

explanation: A representative must disclose in writing his name and the intermediary or intermediaries for which he acts; any change must be communicated in writing at the next dealing after the change.

stem: Which statement correctly contrasts needs selling with product selling?

options.A: Needs selling assumes the client wants your product and creates buying pressure
options.B: Needs selling is service-oriented and relationship-based, discovering the client's needs before advising
options.C: Product selling spends more time on the client's situation than the product
options.D: Both approaches are identical in outcome

explanation: Needs selling is service-oriented, not pressure selling, and relationship-based: you discover the client's needs and advise on the most suitable product and amount. Product selling assumes the client needs your product.

stem: Which of the following correctly lists the order of the needs-analysis process?

options.A: Product recommendations, fact-finding, identifying needs, review, presenting
options.B: Presenting, fact-finding, review, quantifying, recommending
options.C: Fact-finding, identifying and quantifying needs, product recommendations, presenting recommendations, review
options.D: Review, fact-finding, presenting, quantifying, recommending

explanation: The process runs: fact-finding, identifying and quantifying needs, product recommendations, presenting recommendations, then review. Fact-finding via a Fact-Find Document is a MAS 120 requirement.

stem: A client ticks Application Type 3 on the Fact-Find Document. What does this mean?

options.A: The client had a full comprehensive needs analysis
options.B: The client had a partial, specific-needs analysis
options.C: The client waived all disclosure requirements
options.D: The client did NOT undergo any needs analysis and bears responsibility for suitability, but the representative must still explain product features, fees and charges

explanation: Application Type 3 means no needs analysis was done and it is the client's own responsibility to ensure suitability; the representative must still explain product features, fees and charges, and the client must acknowledge the type.

stem: Regarding the deferred period for Disability Income Insurance, which client generally needs cover to start SOONER (a shorter deferred period)?

options.A: A self-employed person whose income stops when he cannot work
options.B: An employee who may keep receiving salary for a period
options.C: An unemployed person
options.D: A retiree living on savings

explanation: A self-employed person needs cover sooner (a shorter deferred period) because his income stops immediately; an employee may keep receiving pay and can accept a longer deferred period. DII is not issued to the unemployed.

stem: Which type of Health Insurance pays ON TOP of all other Health Insurance plans and is NOT subject to the Co-ordination of Benefit Clause?

options.A: Medical Expense Insurance
options.B: Hospital Cash Insurance
options.C: Integrated Shield Plan
options.D: Group Medical Expense Insurance

explanation: Hospital Cash Insurance pays a fixed benefit on top of all other health plans and is not subject to co-ordination of benefits, whereas Medical Expense Insurance is subject to the Co-ordination of Benefit Clause.

stem: Under the Co-ordination of Benefit Clause, when a bill is partly paid by a first plan, the amount claimable from the second plan is:

options.A: The full amount covered under the second plan regardless of the balance
options.B: The maximum of the balance bill or the second plan's cover
options.C: The minimum of the balance bill or the amount covered under the second plan
options.D: Half of the original bill

explanation: The second plan pays the lower of the balance bill (total less what the first plan paid) or its own coverable amount, so total recovery never exceeds actual expenses.

stem: In quantifying disability income protection needs, Method 1 bases the requirement on what figure?

options.A: 100% of monthly income less existing disability benefit
options.B: A lump sum TPD benefit under a Life policy
options.C: Total monthly expenses only
options.D: 75% of monthly income less existing disability benefit

explanation: Method 1 caps the disability income need at 75% of monthly income less existing disability benefit. Method 2 uses total monthly expenses less existing benefit; Method 3 provides a lump-sum TPD benefit.

stem: In Method 3 (lump-sum TPD approach), which existing policies may be deducted from the funds required?

options.A: Only existing policies that carry a TPD benefit, such as Group Term Life or DPS
options.B: Any existing insurance policy
options.C: Only Medical Expense policies
options.D: No existing policies may ever be deducted

explanation: Only existing policies with a TPD benefit (for example Group Term Life or the Dependants' Protection Scheme) may be deducted from the funds required in Method 3.

stem: Which statement about Critical Illness benefit types is correct?

options.A: The Additional Benefit Type lasts for life; the Acceleration Benefit Type ceases at 65
options.B: The Additional Benefit Type normally ceases at age 65; the Acceleration Benefit Type (usually attached to Whole Life) lasts for life
options.C: Both types cease at age 65
options.D: Both types last for life

explanation: The Additional Benefit Type CI normally ceases at age 65, whereas the Acceleration Benefit Type, usually attached to a Whole Life policy, lasts for life.

stem: Which Application Type corresponds to a FULL fact-find where the client discloses relevant information for comprehensive planning and wants a recommendation?

options.A: Application Type 3
options.B: Application Type 2
options.C: Application Type 1
options.D: None of the above

explanation: Application Type 1 is a full fact-find for comprehensive planning where the client wants a recommendation. Type 2 is a partial fact-find for specific needs; Type 3 involves no needs analysis.

stem: Which is NOT one of the three basic principles to observe before recommending a product?

options.A: Recommend products only if the client needs them
options.B: Recommend only the most suitable products for his circumstances
options.C: If he needs a product the company does not carry, tell him so he can find alternatives
options.D: Always recommend the product with the highest commission

explanation: The three principles are: recommend only if needed, recommend only the most suitable products, and if the needed product is not carried, tell the client. Chasing commission is not a principle.

stem: Why should a representative flag Group Insurance cover when reviewing a client's existing protection?

options.A: Group Insurance is not portable and may be lost on leaving the organisation
options.B: Group Insurance is fully portable and permanent
options.C: Group Insurance always duplicates individual cover exactly
options.D: Group Insurance cannot be co-ordinated with individual cover

explanation: Group Insurance is not portable and may be lost when the client leaves the employer, so the representative should flag the gap that would then arise.

stem: A hospital bill is S$22,400. The client's Group Medical Expense plan has already paid S$11,000, and his Private Medical Insurance (PMI) covers S$12,000 of the bill. Applying the Co-ordination of Benefit Clause, how much can he claim from the PMI?
explanation: The PMI pays the lower of the balance bill (22,400 - 11,000 = S$11,400) or its coverable amount (S$12,000). That is S$11,400, so total recovery is exactly S$22,400 and does not exceed the actual expenses.

stem: A client incurs a S$30,000 hospital bill. His group plan pays S$18,000 and his individual Medical Expense plan covers S$15,000 of the bill. Under the Co-ordination of Benefit Clause, what will the individual plan pay?
explanation: The individual plan pays the lower of the balance bill (30,000 - 18,000 = S$12,000) or its coverable amount (S$15,000), which is S$12,000. Total recovery is S$30,000, matching the actual expense.

stem: A health-gap analysis agrees the client needs S$200,000 of Critical Illness cover. He already holds a S$80,000 CI rider. What is the CI shortfall to be recommended?
explanation: The shortfall equals the agreed CI cover less the current CI cover held: 200,000 - 80,000 = S$120,000. Only the shortfall should be recommended to avoid over-insurance.

stem: In the case study, the most suitable policy to meet the working breadwinner's maintenance cost is Disability Income Insurance set at 75% of his S$6,000 monthly salary. What monthly benefit is recommended, and with what deferred period?

options.A: S$4,500, with a deferred period matching how long the employer keeps paying salary (six months)
options.B: S$6,000, with no deferred period
options.C: S$3,000, with a two-year deferred period
options.D: S$4,500, with a lifetime deferred period

explanation: DII is recommended at 75% of the S$6,000 salary, that is S$4,500, with a deferred period matched to how long the employer keeps paying salary, here six months.

stem: A non-working spouse (housewife) needs disability protection. Why is Disability Income Insurance NOT recommended for her, and what is used instead?

options.A: DII is too expensive; a Medical Expense plan is used instead
options.B: She is ineligible for DII with no income and no job; TPD under a Life policy or a Personal Accident policy is used instead
options.C: DII is only for retirees; a Hospital Cash plan is used instead
options.D: She is ineligible; only an emergency fund is recommended

explanation: DII requires an income and a stable job, so a housewife is ineligible; her disability cover is provided through the TPD benefit under a Life policy or a Personal Accident policy.

stem: When computing the present value of maintenance income needs, which rate of return is used to select the annuity factor?

options.A: The nominal rate of return, ignoring inflation
options.B: The inflation rate alone
options.C: The real (inflation-adjusted) rate, being the nominal return less inflation
options.D: The risk-free CPF Ordinary Account rate

explanation: The real rate of return, nominal return minus inflation, is used. In the case a 5% return less 2% inflation gives a 3% real rate, which selects the annuity factor.

stem: Why is Group Hospital & Surgical cover treated as a TEMPORARY rather than lifetime benefit in the case study?

options.A: Because it always expires at age 55
options.B: Because group premiums are always higher than individual premiums
options.C: Because group cover cannot be co-ordinated with individual cover
options.D: Because it is not portable and may be lost or changed when the employee changes jobs or retires

explanation: Group H&S cover is not portable and can be lost or changed on job change or retirement, so it is treated as temporary. Once lost, any co-payments on the individual plan must be met out-of-pocket.

stem: In the case study, why is a 100% Acceleration Benefit Type Critical Illness policy packaged with a Whole Life policy recommended for clients who already have death protection?

options.A: So that cover lasts for life, and for a non-working spouse it also provides the needed TPD cover
options.B: Because it is cheaper than any standalone CI plan
options.C: Because Acceleration CI ceases at age 65 like the Additional type
options.D: Because it avoids the need for any needs analysis

explanation: Acceleration CI attached to Whole Life gives lifelong cover, unlike the Additional Benefit type which ceases at 65, and for a non-working spouse it also delivers the required TPD cover.

stem: Which statement about Group Insurance in the case study is correct?

options.A: Group Insurance carries the same 14-day free-look period as individual plans
options.B: There is no free-look period for any Group Insurance policy
options.C: The insurer may quote before the GIFF Form is signed
options.D: Claims history has little bearing on the group premium

explanation: No free-look period applies to any Group Insurance policy. The insurer cannot quote until the Group Insurance Fact-Finding Form is completed and signed by both client and representative, and past claims history is very important.

stem: For setting a Group Term Life sum assured, which comparison of the two common methods is correct?

options.A: The ranking method reflects length of service better than the salary-multiple method
options.B: Both methods produce identical sums assured
options.C: The ranking method is simpler but ignores tenure; the salary-multiple method is more equitable because it reflects length of service
options.D: The salary-multiple method is simpler and ignores tenure

explanation: The ranking method is easier to manage but ignores length of service; the salary-multiple method reflects tenure (more experienced staff earn more) and is generally more equitable.

stem: In the case study, why was Long-Term Care cover NOT proposed even though it was a valid need?

options.A: Because the client was too young to qualify
options.B: Because the client already held sufficient LTC cover
options.C: Because LTC is never recommended for families
options.D: Because there was no spare premium within the client's stated budget after other priorities

explanation: The recommended package had to fit the client's stated budget; total cash premium of S$695.50 stayed within the S$700 budget, leaving no spare premium for Long-Term Care cover.

stem: A non-working spouse needs S$1,500 a month to maintain living expenses for 21 years. Using a real rate of return of 3% (5% return less 2% inflation), the present-value annuity factor is 15.8775. There is no existing TPD insurance. What TPD sum assured is required?
explanation: Yearly income needed = S$1,500 x 12 = S$18,000. Funds required = S$18,000 x 15.8775 = S$285,795, less S$0 existing TPD insurance = S$285,795.

stem: Using the same figures (yearly income need S$18,000 over 21 years at a 3% real return, factor 15.8775), but the client already holds a Group Term Life policy with a S$120,000 TPD benefit, what additional TPD cover is required?
explanation: Funds required = S$18,000 x 15.8775 = S$285,795. Only existing policies with a TPD benefit may be deducted, so 285,795 - 120,000 = S$165,795 additional cover is needed.

stem: A Singapore Citizen chooses a Class B1 ward at a public hospital but later a friend takes a Class C ward at the same hospital. Comparing the Government subsidy the two receive, which statement is correct?

options.A: The B1 patient gets up to 80% while the C patient gets 20%
options.B: Both wards attract the same subsidy because both are subsidised classes
options.C: The C patient gets up to 80% while the B1 patient gets 20%
options.D: Neither ward is subsidised because both patients chose their own class

explanation: Class B2 and C wards enjoy heavy subsidies of up to 80%, whereas a Class B1 admission is subsidised at only 20%. The patient in the lower-amenity C ward therefore receives the larger subsidy of the two.

stem: Under Notice No: MAS 117, which pair correctly states the minimum structured CPD requirement on MediShield Life or shield plan content and the record retention period?

options.A: 4 hours per calendar year; records kept for 3 years
options.B: 2 hours per calendar year; records kept for 5 years
options.C: 2 hours every two years; records kept for 5 years
options.D: 8 hours per calendar year; records kept for 7 years

explanation: MAS 117 requires a minimum of 2 hours of structured CPD training on shield plan content before the end of each calendar year, and written records must be retained for a period of 5 years.

stem: Under the enhanced migrant worker Medical Insurance requirements, which statement about Stage 1 (from 1 July 2023) is correct?

options.A: The annual claim limit is at least S$60,000, and for claim amounts above S$15,000 insurers pay 75% and employers 25%
options.B: The annual claim limit is at least S$15,000, and for claim amounts above S$60,000 insurers pay 25% and employers 75%
options.C: The annual claim limit is at least S$60,000, and insurers pay 25% while employers pay 75% above S$15,000
options.D: The annual claim limit is at least S$35,000, split equally between insurer and employer

explanation: Stage 1 raised the annual claim limit to at least S$60,000, and for the portion of a claim above S$15,000 the insurer co-pays 75% while the employer co-pays 25%. Reversing the split or the two dollar figures is the trap.

stem: An insured can no longer do his own job but could still perform a different job for which his education and experience suit him, and he can also still perform any occupation at all. Under which total disability definition is he LEAST likely to receive a benefit?

options.A: Any Occupation
options.B: Modified Own Occupation
options.C: Own Occupation
options.D: Severe Disability (ADL-based)

explanation: Any Occupation is the most restrictive definition, requiring inability to perform any occupation whatsoever, so a person who can still work in some job would not qualify. Own Occupation is the most generous and would more readily pay.

stem: Under the Limitation of Disability Benefit Clause, which payment does NOT reduce the monthly disability income benefit payable?

options.A: Work Injury Compensation payments
options.B: Continuing commission from the insured's own occupation
options.C: TPD benefit paid under a separate Life policy
options.D: Monthly benefit from another disability income policy

explanation: The clause reduces the benefit by amounts from other disability policies, Work Injury Compensation and any continuing salary or commission, but TPD benefits paid under a Life policy are expressly excluded from that reduction.

stem: Comparing ElderShield 300, ElderShield 400 and CareShield Life, which statement is correct?

options.A: ElderShield 300 pays S$300 a month for 72 months while CareShield Life pays for 60 months
options.B: All three pay only for a fixed maximum term of 60 or 72 months
options.C: CareShield Life pays a one-time lump sum whereas ElderShield pays monthly
options.D: ElderShield 400 pays S$400 a month for 72 months while CareShield Life pays for the entire duration of severe disability

explanation: ElderShield 300 pays S$300 a month for 60 months and ElderShield 400 pays S$400 a month for 72 months, while CareShield Life pays out for the entire duration the insured remains severely disabled rather than for a capped term.

stem: A severely disabled Singapore Citizen aged 45 wants to draw the maximum monthly cash under MediSave Care. What is the maximum monthly withdrawal and the minimum MediSave balance needed to reach it?

options.A: S$150 per month with a balance of S$10,000 or more
options.B: S$200 per month with a balance of S$20,000 or more
options.C: S$300 per month with a balance of S$15,000 or more
options.D: S$200 per month with a balance of S$5,000 or more

explanation: MediSave Care allows a maximum cash withdrawal of S$200 per month, and that maximum requires a MediSave balance of S$20,000 or more. A balance below S$5,000 means no withdrawal is available at all.

stem: An insured entitled to a standard B1 ward is admitted to a private hospital. Covered charges are S$30,000, the pro-ration factor is 40%, the annual deductible is S$3,500 and co-insurance is 10%. Applying the steps in the correct order, how much does the insurer pay?
explanation: Pro-rate first: 40% of S$30,000 is S$12,000. Subtract the S$3,500 deductible to get S$8,500, then subtract 10% co-insurance (S$850) to reach S$7,650. Deducting the deductible before pro-rating, or skipping the deductible, produces the higher wrong figures.

stem: An insured has a per annum deductible of S$2,500 and 10% co-insurance. Earlier in the same policy year he already incurred S$1,500 of eligible expenses that fell within the deductible. He is now admitted with a S$9,000 bill fully within his policy limits. How much will the insurer pay for this admission?
explanation: The remaining deductible is S$2,500 minus the S$1,500 already met, i.e. S$1,000. Claimable is S$9,000 minus S$1,000 = S$8,000; co-insurance of 10% is S$800, so the insurer pays S$7,200. Ignoring the earlier expenses or forgetting the co-insurance gives the other figures.

stem: Fiona is insured for a total disability monthly benefit of S$6,000 with a 5% per annum escalation benefit. After one full year of continuous total disability the benefit escalates, and she then returns to work earning S$2,000 a month against pre-disability earnings of S$8,000. Applying escalation before the partial disability formula, what monthly benefit does she now receive?
explanation: Escalate first: 5% of S$6,000 is S$300, giving S$6,300. The partial disability factor is (8,000 minus 2,000) divided by 8,000 = 0.75, so 0.75 times S$6,300 = S$4,725. Skipping the escalation gives S$4,500, and using 3% escalation gives S$4,635.

stem: An insured holds a S$300,000 Whole Life policy with a 60% Acceleration Benefit CI rider and later a S$120,000 Additional Benefit CI rider on the same life. He is diagnosed with one covered CI. Ignoring bonuses, what is paid on diagnosis and what basic sum assured remains for a later death claim?

options.A: S$300,000 paid on CI, with nothing left for death
options.B: S$180,000 from the acceleration plus S$120,000 from the additional benefit paid on CI, with S$120,000 basic sum assured left for death
options.C: S$120,000 paid on CI, with S$300,000 left for death
options.D: S$420,000 paid on CI, with S$300,000 left for death

explanation: The acceleration pre-pays 60% of the S$300,000 basic, that is S$180,000, drawn out of the basic sum assured, leaving S$120,000 of basic for a later death claim. The additional benefit rider pays its S$120,000 on top without touching the basic. So S$180,000 plus S$120,000 is paid on diagnosis and S$120,000 of basic remains for death.

stem: Under the LIA Critical Illness Framework 2019, which statement about how definitions are standardised is correct?

options.A: LIA sets common definitions for the severe stage of the listed conditions, while insurers set their own definitions for the mildly to moderately severe or extremely severe stages
options.B: LIA sets common definitions for every stage of all covered conditions, leaving insurers no discretion
options.C: Insurers set the severe-stage definitions and LIA only reviews the early-stage ones
options.D: LIA reviews the common definitions once every ten years and covers 30 conditions

explanation: For the 37 listed conditions LIA standardises only the severe-stage definition; insurers apply their own definitions for the mildly to moderately severe or extremely severe stages, and for conditions not on the list. The definitions are reviewed once every three years, not ten.

stem: A client wants a CI plan that can pay more than once, including for a relapse or a different condition arising later. Which arrangement meets this need, and how does it differ from a traditional acceleration plan?

options.A: An Additional Benefit rider, which by design always pays several times
options.B: A stand-alone Term CI policy, which pays repeatedly until expiry
options.C: A Multiple Pay CI plan, which allows second and subsequent claims subject to waiting periods, unlike a traditional or acceleration plan that pays only once
options.D: A single acceleration plan, which resets its sum assured after each claim

explanation: Only a Multiple Pay CI plan allows a second and subsequent claim, including relapse, recurrence or a different condition, subject to applicable waiting periods. Traditional and acceleration CI plans allow only one claim, and an additional benefit rider on its own does not confer multi-claim ability.

stem: For a Class A ward bill under MediShield Life, in what order are pro-ration, the claim limits, the deductible and co-insurance applied?

options.A: Deductible first, then co-insurance, then pro-ration, then the claim limits
options.B: Pro-ration first to the Class B2/C equivalent, then the claim limits, then the deductible, then co-insurance
options.C: Claim limits first, then the deductible, then pro-ration, then co-insurance
options.D: Co-insurance first, then the deductible, then the claim limits, then pro-ration

explanation: The higher-ward bill is pro-rated down to the Class B2/C equivalent first, then capped by the daily and surgical claim limits, then the deductible is subtracted, and finally co-insurance is applied to the amount above the deductible by band. Applying the deductible or co-insurance before pro-ration would overstate the payout.

stem: A financial adviser contrasts CareShield Life with ElderShield400 for a client. Which pair of statements is correct?

options.A: CareShield Life pays for a maximum of 72 months, whereas ElderShield400 pays for life
options.B: Both pay at least S$600 per month, and both cap payouts at 60 months
options.C: CareShield Life pays at least S$600 per month for as long as severe disability lasts with no duration cap, whereas ElderShield400 pays S$400 per month for up to 72 months
options.D: CareShield Life premiums are payable for life, whereas ElderShield400 premiums stop at age 67

explanation: CareShield Life pays at least S$600 per month for as long as severe disability persists, with no cap on payout duration, while ElderShield400 pays S$400 per month for up to 72 months. CareShield Life premiums are payable until age 67 or for 10 years, whichever is longer, not for life.

stem: A patient with an Integrated Shield Plan is hospitalised. Given that the IP insurer and the CPF Board each compute a payout, and given the MOH claims protocol, which statement is correct?

options.A: The eventual payout is the sum of the IP benefit and the MediShield Life benefit, and MediSave is drawn before any insurance
options.B: The eventual payout is the average of the two benefits, and MediFund is drawn before MediSave
options.C: The eventual payout is the lower of the two benefits, and cash is always drawn first
options.D: The eventual payout is the higher of the IP benefit and the MediShield Life benefit, and the claims order is third party or employer, then MediShield Life or IP, then MediSave, then cash

explanation: To avoid duplication the eventual payout is the higher of the IP benefit and the MediShield Life benefit, not the sum, average or lower. The MOH claims protocol pays in the order of third party or employer or private insurance first, then MediShield Life or IP, then MediSave, then cash.

stem: A client asks why his adviser cannot let him pay his new Integrated Shield Plan rider premium from MediSave and why the rider no longer covers his entire co-payment. Which explanation is correct?

options.A: Riders are MediSave-approved up to the Additional Withdrawal Limit, and full riders were retained to reduce over-consumption
options.B: Riders are cash-only and not MediSave-approved, and from 8 March 2018 new riders must leave a co-payment of at least 5% to curb over-consumption
options.C: Riders are fully MediSave-payable, and the minimum co-payment was set at 10%
options.D: Riders may be paid from MediSave up to S$600, and the co-payment must be at least 3%

explanation: IP riders are not MediSave-approved and can only be paid in cash. From 8 March 2018 new riders must impose a co-payment of 5% or more, since full riders that covered the entire co-payment encouraged over-consumption of healthcare.

stem: An insurer wants a renewal basis under which it can decline renewal only for reasons unrelated to the insured's health, such as the insured reaching a specified age or leaving a defined occupation, while still being able to raise the premium. Which basis is this?

options.A: Guaranteed Renewable
options.B: Cancellable
options.C: Conditionally Renewable
options.D: Non-renewable

explanation: Conditionally Renewable lets the insurer decline renewal only under specified conditions unrelated to health, such as age or employment, and it may also raise the premium. Guaranteed Renewable permits non-renewal only for non-payment, while Cancellable lets the insurer terminate at any time for any reason.

stem: A Singapore Citizen aged 55 is admitted to a Class B2 ward for 12 days at S$900 per day (S$10,800 actual), with no surgery. Using Appendix 9B figures (Normal Ward limit S$800 per day, deductible S$2,000, co-insurance 10%/5%/3%), how much does MediShield Life pay?
explanation: Claimable is capped at S$800 x 12 = S$9,600, below the S$10,800 actual. Less the S$2,000 deductible leaves S$7,600. Co-insurance: the first S$5,000 band less the deductible is S$3,000 at 10% = S$300; the amount from S$5,000 to S$9,600 is S$4,600 at 5% = S$230; total S$530. Payout = S$9,600 - S$2,000 - S$530 = S$7,070.

stem: A patient with an Integrated Shield Plan rider (minimum 5% co-payment, co-payment cap S$3,000 per policy year) receives panel, pre-authorised treatment costing S$80,000. What is the patient's co-payment?
explanation: Five per cent of S$80,000 is S$4,000, which exceeds the S$3,000 per policy year cap for panel, pre-authorised treatment. The co-payment is therefore capped at S$3,000. The cap bites whenever 5% of the bill exceeds S$3,000, that is for bills above S$60,000.

stem: A CareShield Life policyholder began receiving the base payout of S$600 per month in her first year of severe disability. Payouts increase 2% per year in the first five years. Assuming she remains severely disabled, how much does she receive in total during her SECOND year of disability?
explanation: In the second year the monthly payout rises 2% from S$600 to S$600 x 1.02 = S$612. Over 12 months that is S$612 x 12 = S$7,344. The unadjusted figure of S$7,200 ignores the 2% annual increase.

stem: A Singapore Citizen aged 70 stays in a Class A ward (pro-ration factor 35%). Daily ward and treatment charges are S$1,000 per day for 15 days (S$15,000), and a Table 5C surgical procedure is charged at S$9,000. Using Appendix 9B (Normal Ward limit S$800 per day, Table 5C surgical limit S$2,180, deductible S$2,000, co-insurance 10%/5%/3%), what does MediShield Life pay?
explanation: Pro-rate at 35%: ward S$15,000 becomes S$5,250 (below the S$800 x 15 = S$12,000 limit, so claimable S$5,250); surgery S$9,000 becomes S$3,150 but is capped at the Table 5C limit of S$2,180. Total claimable S$5,250 + S$2,180 = S$7,430. Less the S$2,000 deductible leaves S$5,430. Co-insurance: the first S$5,000 band less deductible is S$3,000 at 10% = S$300, and S$5,000 to S$7,430 is S$2,430 at 5% = S$121.50, total S$421.50. Payout = S$7,430 - S$2,000 - S$421.50 = S$5,008.50.

stem: A group Health Insurance portfolio reports paid claims of S$400,000 and pending claims of S$60,000 for the year, but the actuary has NOT yet added any estimate for claims that have occurred but are not yet reported. What is the most likely consequence for pricing if this omission is left uncorrected?

options.A: The incurred claims will be understated and the premium set too low to cover eventual liabilities
options.B: The incurred claims will be overstated and the premium set too high
options.C: There is no effect because unreported claims are never the insurer's liability
options.D: Investment income will automatically offset any shortfall

explanation: Total claims comprise paid, pending and Incurred But Not Reported (IBNR) claims. Leaving out the IBNR estimate understates incurred claims, so the premium would be set too low and reserves would be insufficient for the eventual liabilities.

stem: A block of Health Insurance business earned S$2,000,000 of premium in the year. Paid claims were S$1,050,000, pending claims S$150,000 and estimated IBNR S$120,000. What is the incurred claims (loss) ratio, and how does it compare with a target ceiling of 65%?

options.A: 60.0%; within the 65% target
options.B: 66.0%; above the 65% target
options.C: 65.0%; exactly at the target
options.D: 55.5%; within the 65% target

explanation: Incurred claims = 1,050,000 + 150,000 + 120,000 = S$1,320,000. Ratio = 1,320,000 / 2,000,000 = 66.0%, which is above the 65% ceiling. Excluding IBNR would wrongly give 60.0% and mask the breach.

stem: An insurer markets a Hospital Income plan online, asking the applicant only three health questions whose answers decide acceptance, with no medical examination. Which underwriting method is this, and what is the usual trade-off?

options.A: Guaranteed Issuance Offer, which asks no questions at all
options.B: Full Medical Underwriting, which gives certainty of cover from the start
options.C: Simplified Issuance Offer, giving quick cover but at a higher premium for the risk taken on
options.D: Moratorium Underwriting, which excludes pre-existing conditions for two to five years

explanation: Asking a few questions whose answers determine approval with no medical exam describes a Simplified Issuance Offer. Cover is granted quickly compared with days or weeks under full underwriting, but the premium is higher because the insurer takes on more unknown risk. A method asking no questions at all would instead be a Guaranteed Issuance Offer.

stem: A 40-member group Disability Income plan sets a free cover limit. One senior manager's proposed benefit exceeds that limit. What must happen to his cover above the free cover limit?

options.A: The entire group must be re-underwritten from scratch
options.B: Only the portion of his benefit exceeding the free cover limit must be individually underwritten
options.C: His whole benefit is automatically granted because he belongs to the group
options.D: His benefit is capped at the free cover limit and the excess is declined outright

explanation: The free cover limit is the maximum coverage granted to each member without a health declaration. Coverage up to the limit is granted automatically, but the excess above it must be individually underwritten, which may require the member to complete a health declaration or medical examination.

stem: An underwriter assesses a Disability Income proposal as needing more than 50% extra premium and instead offers to cap the benefit period at five years. Which category of underwriting decision is this?

options.A: A specific exclusion endorsement
options.B: A postponement of the risk
options.C: A modification of benefits
options.D: An outright decline

explanation: Capping the benefit period, reducing the monthly benefit or lengthening the deferred period are all modifications of benefits. A specific exclusion names a particular risk that will not be paid, a postponement offers no terms now but reconsiders later, and a decline offers no cover at all.

stem: An employed applicant earns a basic salary of S$5,000 a month and already holds an existing Disability Income policy paying S$1,200 a month. Applying the income-replacement ceiling, what is the maximum ADDITIONAL monthly Disability Income benefit an insurer will typically allow?
explanation: The benefit is capped at 75% of current income: 0.75 x S$5,000 = S$3,750 total. Deducting the existing S$1,200 already in force leaves S$3,750 - S$1,200 = S$2,550 of additional benefit the insurer will allow.

stem: Under Part I of Notice No: MAS 120, which Division sets out the requirements on the provision of advice relating to A&H policies, including the Know-Your-Client and needs-analysis obligations?

options.A: Division 1A
options.B: Division 3
options.C: Division 4
options.D: Division 6

explanation: Division 4 covers requirements on the provision of advice for A&H policies: reasonable basis for advice, Know-Your-Client, needs analysis, documentation and record keeping, and switching. Division 1A deals with disclosure, Division 3 with additional disclosure by direct insurers, and Division 6 with offences.

stem: A direct insurer plans to vary the terms of an individual Medical Expense policy and to reissue the product summary. Which pair of MAS 120 requirements applies?

options.A: Furnish the change in writing at least 14 days beforehand, in any legible 8-point font
options.B: Furnish the change in writing at least 30 days beforehand, in Times New Roman 10-point or larger
options.C: Furnish the change verbally at renewal, in Arial 12-point or larger
options.D: Furnish the change in writing at least 60 days beforehand, in Calibri 11-point or larger

explanation: The insurer must disclose the existing and new terms in writing to the policy owner at least 30 days before the change takes effect, and the product summary, conditional offer letter or termination letter for an individual Medical Expense policy must use a font size of Times New Roman 10-point or larger.

stem: A client needs S$2,000 a month to maintain his dependants' living expenses for 20 years should he become totally and permanently disabled. Using a real rate of return of 3% the present-value annuity factor is 15.3238. He already holds a Group Term Life policy with a S$150,000 TPD benefit. What ADDITIONAL TPD sum assured is required?
explanation: Yearly income needed = S$2,000 x 12 = S$24,000. Funds required = S$24,000 x 15.3238 = S$367,771. Only existing policies carrying a TPD benefit may be deducted, so S$367,771 - S$150,000 = S$217,771 of additional cover is needed.
